Alright, so notify your property owner in writing that you intend to move out by a specified date (you will move out before that, but that doesn't matter). Pay your rent as designated by your lease.

When you leave, take a lot of pictures, take a video recording of your walkthrough, etc. If you can get your property owner to do a walkthrough with you, even better.

Then get familiar with the relevant state civil code regarding security deposits, which states (as a summary):

The law requires all property owners to return a tenant's security deposit within 21 days of move-out either in full or partially. If any deductions are taken from the tenant's security deposit, the partial refund check must be accompanied by: (1) a written itemized statement that lists the amounts deducted from the security deposit and the reasons for the deductions, and (2) if the deduction exceeds a certain amount, copies of receipts for the charges incurred to repair or clean the unit. Make sure you provide your property owner with your new address. If you did not provide your property owner with your new address in your written notice of intent to vacate, write down your new address on any move-out inspection checklist, or email your new address to the property owner shortly thereafter.

If the security deposit is not returned within 21 days, if the tenant disagrees with the amounts deducted, or if the tenant did not receive an itemization accompanied by receipts, the tenant should send a letter to the property owner via certified mail return receipt requested. If the property owner does not respond within a reasonable time (7 to 10 days), the tenant should then file a claim in Small Claims Court for the actual security deposit withheld and statutory damages of two times that amount pursuant to the relevant civil code. Consider meeting with an attorney prior to filing for advice on preparation and presentation of your claim.

I placed the call. My knuckles were white as I whispered into the handset. “Are we ready to go?”

“Yea,” came the response. “I finished it late last night. Whenever you are ready on your side.”

I hesitated. I did love that place. I didn’t wish it any ill will, but what I planned would cause panic, terror. Maybe even death.

I hung up the phone. I just couldn’t do it, not yet. A heavy sigh escaped my chest while I put on my coat. The slick finish on the outside would cut the wind, but do nothing against the cold. Locking my door, I fumbled and dropped my keys. I bent to pick them up, but got distracted by a call on my phone.

“We are ready to go. Give the word!” The voice was annoyed, higher pitched than before, but still my same man. “You had me spend 5 months on this idiot project. You hounded me daily for updates, projections. And now you wait?”

“I’m in charge here! It is my money, my plan! You are doing pretty ok now because of me!” If he was annoyed, I was even worse now. “You’ll wait till I am good and ready.”

I walked. 30 minutes, 2 miles, a good pace. By then I was in the business district. In the Wednesday afternoon, there was a good bustle but nothing crazy. All around me, activity. People, cars, horns, noise. Prosperity, despair, richness and ruin. I couldn’t.

A screech, a horn, and a crash. I turned to the noise, and saw the traffic light had turned off. All down the avenue, more fender benders, more lights out. He had done it on his own. No backup had been built in, no fail-safe. A few people came out the revolving door near me, looking around confused. Their buildings were dark as well. The sirens began, first from a few cop cars, but then from every building. Each one that had an emergency alarm had a stream of people, turning into a torrent, flooding out. Fire alarms began. I stood there in the cacophony, unable to help, but knowing what had happened.

The program wasn’t permanent. It would only last 2 or 3 weeks, or maybe a week if they could figure it out quick. It was already in the backups, so no worries there. And the real lynchpin was the local leader. I knew that person could not possibly deal with any major catastrophe. Any damage I had paid that disgruntled employee to inflict would be multiplied tenfold by botched relief efforts, mismanaged resources, and occasional malevolent neglect.

I walked home. No use trying to catch the train.
